anti_generic_signature_read: Blind, asked what was memorable rather than generic: 'the pieces are actual planets as solids, not tokens with planet pictures on them, and they are correctly differentiated by SIZE as well as colour... the board's hierarchy is legible before you know a single rule. Saturn's ring is the signature silhouette of the whole set and the one piece you would pick up first. The terrain is the second memorable thing: real recessed crater dishes and a genuinely sunken black pit tile, not printed graphics -- you can feel the board with your thumb.' Against it, blind: the four pale spheres with no silhouette of their own, one cone primitive reused everywhere, the unreadable disc numerals, and -- in round one only -- that Saturn was 'under-painted'. It withdrew that last one in round two; the others are carried into product.json.
blind_action_read: 'View-2 is the action shot: three renders of the same board at three different moments, left to right. Left board carries the full sixteen pieces in what looks like a starting or early position. Middle board carries about ten pieces, in different squares... Right board carries about six pieces, with a blue sphere now standing ON the black recessed tile... So the sequence is 16 -> ~10 -> ~6 pieces: material is being captured and removed, and survivors have moved.' Of the close-ups: 'the same design in a white-puck and a black-puck version, and rotated 180 degrees between the two.'
blind_form_read: 'Everything is built out of a very small vocabulary of primitives, stacked. The board is a flat slab... subdivided into individual square tiles separated by thin recessed grooves -- the tiles read as inset panels, not painted graphics.' It separated the terrain by solid form: 'brown/ochre tiles whose surface is dished into shallow concave craters... genuinely recessed below the tile plane -- I count about twelve'; 'cyan tiles with a shallow radial fan or starburst relief and, standing proud of them, slim solid cones'; 'one black tile which is recessed noticeably below the surrounding surface, a pit'. Pieces: 'a thick cylindrical puck -> a short straight cylindrical neck the same colour as the planet -> the sphere, which is flat-cut at the bottom.' Of Saturn: 'a flat annular plate of constant thickness.'
blind_held_read: Unprompted, before knowing anything: 'This is a tabletop board game, rendered in CAD... A flat square/rectangular board is divided into a grid of square tiles... Standing on the tiles are sixteen playing pieces, each a coloured sphere sitting on a short cylindrical puck base -- eight pucks white, eight pucks black, so two players of eight pieces each. The spheres are planets. Off to the upper right... two flat grey trays, each with scalloped semicircular recesses... one tray per player, for pieces off the board. If someone handed me this I would say: it's a planets chess/skirmish game -- spheres on discs, one set light, one set dark, moving across terrain tiles.'
blind_relationship_read: 'Spheres sit on necks, necks sit on pucks, pucks sit one-per-tile on the board -- each puck is centred in its square with clear margin, so occupancy is unambiguous. Tiles tile the board plane; the crater dishes and the black pit are recessed INTO that plane; the cones and the beige pad stand PROUD of it... The two trays sit off the board entirely... they are not a frame or a lid, they are separate furniture. Black-puck pieces and white-puck pieces are interleaved across the board rather than segregated to opposite ends, consistent with a game in progress.'
blind_subjects_read: Named unprompted, with its own confidence on each: 'The pieces are the planets of the solar system, one sphere per body, two copies of each (one on a white puck, one on a black puck).' Jupiter -- very high confidence, 'alternating white and orange bands and a distinct oval red-orange spot'. Saturn -- very high confidence, 'pale cream-yellow banded sphere with a flat tilted ring, the subject of views 3 through 10'. Earth, Mars -- high confidence. Two ice giants, a cream Venus and a small cratered Mercury or Moon at medium to low confidence. It also read the rank ladder without being told it existed: 'correctly differentiated by size as well as colour -- the gas giants are genuinely the big pieces at ~95-100 px against Earth and Mars at ~48-50 px, which means the board's hierarchy is legible before you know a single rule.'

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: BLIND, before anything was revealed and while the critic still believed the softness was a fault: 'no, they do not read the same. Jupiter is markedly louder, busier and higher-contrast than Saturn... Jupiter's band-to-band tonal steps are big enough that you can count its stripes from across the table, and it has a saturated red focal point... Saturn's stripes at the same distance collapse into one flat cream mass.' It put Jupiter's per-band contrast at 'roughly three to four times Saturn's'. PRIMED: 'MET. Knowing the goal does not change the measurement, only its sign... my blind read is the strongest evidence you have that the goal was hit, because I reached Saturn is the quiet one, Jupiter is the loud one with no brief in front of me.'
critical_form_requirements.requirement: 1. Saturn reads softer and quieter than Jupiter when the two are seen together in iso.png.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: PRIMED, counted independently: 'three amber bands north of the ring line... the chocolate band and one further olive-amber band below it. Three north plus two south equals five. View-9, looking straight down the north pole, independently gives three distinct amber annuli... That is a genuine cross-check and it lands on five.' Unequal width MET: '~50, 60 and 40 px, and the chocolate one ~135-145 px... the old 12-degrees-everywhere scheme is plainly gone.' Not symmetric MET: 'three bands north and two south, with the only dark one in the south, cannot be mirror-symmetric.' It refused the exact numbers -- 'I would not accept an image-based claim... Measure them on the solid' -- so they are settled in measure/saturn-atlas-resolution.md: 9, 15, 8, 16, 12 degrees, four different gaps.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: 2. Five bands at +46/+55, +18/+33, +2/+10, -14/-30 and -38/-50 -- widths 9, 15, 8, 16 and 12 degrees -- unequal in width, unequal in spacing, not mirror-symmetric about the equator.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: PRIMED: 'exactly one band is unambiguously a different pigment... Every other band sits in one peach/amber family... Distinguishable: yes, unmistakably. Without dominating: it occupies roughly 355 x 130 px against a globe disc of ~255,000 px2, so about 13% of the visible face -- a minority, and in views 3, 5-near and 9 it is nearly invisible, and in view-1 it is invisible entirely. So it does not dominate the piece.' Its reservation is kept unsoftened in largest_risk: 'It passes, but it is the thing closest to the line.' Measured side: measure/saturn-tone-separation.md, 39.5 luma levels against the globe and 34.7 against the light bands, between the 33.5 accepted on Venus and the 45.5 accepted on Mercury.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: 3. Four bands in one mid tone and at most ONE darker band, cocoa_brown, at -14/-30 -- kept only if distinguishable without dominating.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: PRIMED, and a correction the critic made to its own blind read unprompted. Blind it called the cap edge 'slightly wobbly at the lower left'; re-looking at the same pixels it withdrew that: 'the view-9 wobble is 2-3 px and reads as antialiasing, not lobing... where the cap boundary meets a saturated band and the contrast is high the edge is crisp, smooth and continuously curved, with no lobes, no scallops and no straight segments. So: MET, no ragged rim.' On the latitude it measured rather than accepted -- 'radius ratio 152/272 = 0.559... phi ~ 56.0 degrees... consistent with +58 to within +/-2-3 degrees, but not a confirmation; that is geometry.' Settled on the source: saturn_atlas.CAP_LAT is 58.0, drawn as a plain cap with no lobe list.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: 4. A bright polar region above +58 degrees, in the lightest tone the piece already carries, bounded by an exact parallel with no lobed or ragged rim.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: PRIMED, split honestly. 'The chocolate band is visibly wavy: the boundary between it and the band below undulates by roughly 25-30 px across the globe's width, a clear single-hump S rather than a smooth elliptical arc.' For the rest it declared a confound and declined: 'a true circle of latitude on a globe tilted 26.73 degrees and viewed side-on projects as an ellipse arc, which at 900 px is not reliably distinguishable from a 2-3 degree wave.' It withdrew its blind claim that every edge waved. One point it volunteered our way: down the pole, 'where projection cannot manufacture a wave', the +46/+55 annulus 'reads as a clean circle'. Settled on the source: saturn_atlas.WAVES has four entries, both boundaries of ntb and stb and no others.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: 5. Exactly the two widest bands -- +18/+33 and -14/-30 -- carry a 2.5 degree wave on each boundary; the three narrower bands stay exact circles of latitude.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: PRIMED, and the critic chose the right frame itself: 'the test has to be done at a camera that looks along the lean, and view-5 is that camera, both pieces in one frame. Near piece... a brilliant white ellipse ~170 x 130 px, about 22,000 px2. Far piece... a duller crescent at the upper-left limb, ~95 x 85 px, about 8,000 px2. Same camera, near-identical globe sizes, and the Anti-Sol cap is roughly a third the projected area -- that is much reduced.' It added an unprompted warning we kept: 'views 6 versus 7 and 9 versus 10 do NOT show the reduction... anyone who tries to verify requirement 6 from them will wrongly conclude it failed.' Numbers in measure/saturn-cap-visibility.md: 29,333 against 8,882 pixels at the hero frame, 42,908 against 41,874 down each piece's own pole.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: 6. The cap is on the north only, so at the product's camera it is in plain view on the Sol piece and much reduced on the Anti-Sol one -- the lean, not a mirror failure.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: PRIMED: 'MET on everything observable... the near ring descends left to right while the far piece's ring tip ascends; the near support web sweeps down and right to the disc, while a matching grey web wedge belonging to the far piece peeks out at lower-left. Mirrored, not offset... both caps north, both chocolate bands south, band tones matching, wave crests reading as reflections of each other.' It refused the mechanism -- 'whether the two pieces are genuinely mirrored leans or one object yawed 180 degrees... both produce the identical image. That is geometry.' Settled in measure/saturn-cap-visibility.md role by role: ring, cap and light bands agree to 7.1e-05, 1.4e-03 and 9.6e-04 mm3; the two differences that remain are the designed disc draft and 0.074 mm3 of the dark band buried below the seat line, with the cause measured.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: 7. The two pieces are still mirrors of one another -- same markings, same tones, same cap -- differing only in the lean and in the disc and numeral colours.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: PRIMED: 'ABSENT... View-9 gives the definitive angle: the cap boundary is a circle, centred within 8 px of the globe's centre, with no straight segments, no six-fold flattening and no vertices. View-3 at a high oblique angle shows the same boundary as a smooth continuous arc.' Blind, the same boundary had already been described as smooth and circular with no mention of a hexagon anywhere. The arithmetic for why it is not drawn is in parts/saturn_atlas.NOT_DRAWN: the hexagon's visible edge is 0.49 degrees of arc, 0.11 mm, a quarter of one nozzle width, against a nozzle that needs 1.76 degrees.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NEGATIVE 8a. No hexagonal polar vortex at or near the north pole.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: PRIMED: 'ABSENT. I checked all eight close-ups. Every discrete non-band mark I can find is on the disc, not the globe... Nothing on the spherical surface in any view breaks the banding -- no oval, no closed contour, no blob. This is the clearest contrast with Jupiter, which does carry a spot at ~12x8 px in view-1.' Blind, its own inventory of this piece was bands, a bright pole and a ring, and nothing else; it listed a spot only for Jupiter.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NEGATIVE 8b. No storm, spot, oval or blob anywhere on the globe.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: PRIMED: 'ABSENT. The two face-on-ish views are the test: view-9 shows the ring as a plain white annulus from r ~ 272 to r ~ 330, and view-10 as a plain grey annulus. Neither carries a radial line, a gap, a Cassini-style division or any azimuthal subdivision.' It distinguished the one linear feature it could see on the ring from a division itself: 'it runs ALONG the ring's length, not across it, so it is not a radial division' -- that item is the web faceting dealt with in resolution. Why the divisions are not drawn, with arithmetic, is in parts/saturn_atlas.NOT_DRAWN: Cassini would be 0.15 mm and Encke 0.010 mm of a 2.00 mm printed projection.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NEGATIVE 8c. No spokes, radial lines or divisions of any kind in the ring.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: PRIMED: 'ABSENT. No dark region on any globe follows the ring's straight edge. The chocolate band's boundaries undulate in the same manner as the other band boundaries, which a shadow from a flat circular plate could not do... And view-9, looking straight down the axis where a ring shadow would show as a dark annulus on the globe, shows only warm amber and yellow annuli with no grey ring-shaped darkening.' The critic reached that reasoning BLIND: in round one, not knowing a ring shadow was forbidden, it raised the shadow hypothesis for the dark band itself and rejected it on exactly this evidence.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NEGATIVE 8d. No shadow of the ring printed onto the globe as a marking.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: PRIMED: 'no relief visible... The test is the silhouette where band boundaries cross the limb. View-6 right limb: the arc is smooth and continuous, and the three band boundaries that cross it produce colour changes with no notch, step or bump. View-8 the same on both limbs. View-9's globe outline is a clean circle all the way round.' It refused to call that proof -- 'an inlay proud by a few hundredths of a millimetre would be sub-pixel at 900 px... settle it on the solid' -- so: every region tool in features/patches.py is trimmed against the sphere at RELIEF_DEPTH below the surface and each patch is a split half of the globe itself, and check_overhang passes on both printed parts with zero regions needing support.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NEGATIVE 8e. Nothing protrudes: every marking is a flush colour inlay, the globe's outer surface stays an exact sphere, and no marking adds relief or a downward-facing surface.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: PRIMED, and refused for the right reason: 'CANNOT TELL, and this cannot be settled by images at all... I would reject any image-based claim here in either direction, including a claim that it did change. Diff the geometry.' Diffed in measure/saturn-ring-unchanged.md: all nine values of the ring block quoted against the published numbers and every one unchanged, and both ring occurrences compared against the published assembly at one solid each, 574.192167 and 574.192096 mm3, 0.00e+00 box drift. The critic did withdraw both of its round-one ring calls: 'fully consistent with a fused joint... a 1.00 mm bite booleaned into one solid would look exactly like this', and on the overhang, 'I was wrong and I withdraw it. There is visible solid material under the ring... unbroken from ring to disc.'
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NEGATIVE 8f. Saturn's ring system is unchanged from the published set -- same diameters, same thickness, same web, same parameters.

critical_form_requirements.blind_evidence: PRIMED, and refused: 'CANNOT TELL, same reason... looks unremarkable is not unchanged -- I have no prior render to compare against. This is a file/geometry diff, not an image question, and I would not accept an image-based claim that the rest of the set is untouched.' Diffed twice. measure/occurrence-geometry.md: 196 published labels carrying 216 solids against this run's 200 carrying 220, on solid count, exact volume and bounding box -- 186 identical, the only gone and new labels Saturn's own, and 'nothing outside saturn_sol_* and saturn_anti_* gained, lost or moved a solid'. measure/revision-part-hashes.md: 20 of 24 printed geometries byte-identical, four panels differing only in an exporter occurrence counter verified line by line, and both Saturn parts byte-identical too.
critical_form_requirements.requirement: NEGATIVE 8g. Nothing else in the set changed: the other fourteen worlds, four panels, twelve belt tiles, six corona cells, two stars and two trays are exactly as they were.

largest_risk: The critic's, in its own words and not softened: the one cocoa_brown band. 'It passes, but it is the thing closest to the line, and if anything on this piece gets revisited it should be that band's value rather than its width.' It measured that band as about 13 per cent of the visible face, invisible at the product's own camera, but 'the single loudest mark anywhere on the pale half of your set' in the straight-on elevations. It is kept on measured and rendered evidence: 39.5 luma levels against the globe, between the 33.5 accepted on Venus and the 45.5 accepted on Mercury, and a rendered with/without comparison on BOTH armies in snap/worlds/saturn-dark-band-*.png where the version without it is calmer and also flatter. Second risk, belonging to the set rather than to this correction and not withdrawn: 'Venus, the small cratered world, and the two ice giants are four pale spheres differentiated by colour and a fifth-root size step only, with no silhouette difference and no legible label', and the disc numerals 'resolve as two or three blocky rectangles'. Both are carried into product.json unchanged.
resolution:
PROTOCOL. Ten canonical images copied to a scratch directory as view-1 to view-10 so no path could prime the critic: iso.png, signature.png, and the two Saturn pieces at the three frames the brief asks for -- the product's own azimuth with the ring in projection, along the ring's own plane, and down each piece's own leaning pole. No Wish, no brief, no product name. Round one was fixed before anything was revealed; round two was primed and says so on every line.

OUTCOME. Two rounds, no repair round needed, no geometry changed between them. Round one named the object, named Saturn and Jupiter unaided, read the rank ladder off the globe sizes, and answered the loud-versus-quiet question the right way round while still believing the quietness was a fault. Round two matched every positive and negative requirement and declared seven of the fourteen to be geometry questions it would not settle from pixels; each is settled on the solids and the bytes by the report named in that requirement.

WITHDRAWN. All three of round one's defect calls, on re-examining the same pixels: the ring/globe junction, the ring as an unsupported overhang ('I was wrong and I withdraw it. There is visible solid material under the ring'), and two marks read as stray geometry, which are the far piece's numeral. It also withdrew its blind claim that every band boundary waved.

ONE OPEN ITEM. A dashed line along the ring's top face in the ring-plane views. Lifting the camera 3 degrees does not remove it and three tessellation tolerances give a pixel-identical pattern, so it is the 96 ruled sectors of the ring's web meeting the plate's cylinder: unchanged published geometry, invisible at the product camera, harmless to the print gates, disclosed in product.json rather than repaired, because repairing it means moving the ring.

MOTION is off by the operator's frozen option and is unverified, never passed. print_gate_sha256s is empty and the product is digitally-verified-not-print-ready.
reviewer: One independent native critic, given ten canonical images under neutral names and nothing else -- no Wish, no brief, no product name. Its blind read was fixed before anything was revealed.
